# Non-Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models {#sec-nar-lm}

Every text model in this book so far generates left to right, one token
conditioned on all the tokens before it. @sec-diffusion showed that images
generate the opposite way, denoising the whole field in parallel. This chapter
asks whether text can too, and surveys the non-autoregressive lineage that
tries. By the end a reader can explain why parallel text generation is
attractive, why it historically lost quality to autoregression, how discrete
diffusion revived it, and why the frontier stays autoregressive despite a 2025
wave of fast diffusion language models.

## The appeal and its cost

Autoregression is serial: generating $n$ tokens takes $n$ sequential forward
passes, each waiting on the last. Non-autoregressive generation produces the
tokens in parallel instead. Gu et al. first did this for translation, reporting
an order-of-magnitude lower latency at a cost of as little as two BLEU points
against the autoregressive teacher it distilled from [@gu2017nar]. The cost has a
cause: emitting tokens independently throws away the dependencies between them,
so the model cannot tell which of several valid outputs it is committing to, the
"multimodality" problem. Iterative refinement buys much of the quality back.
Mask-Predict decodes in parallel, then over a constant number of rounds masks out
and re-predicts the tokens it is least confident about, reaching within about one
BLEU of a left-to-right transformer while decoding faster
[@ghazvininejad2019maskpredict]. Predict-in-parallel, then refine: that pattern
is the bridge to diffusion.

## Diffusion for discrete text

D3PM generalized diffusion to discrete data, replacing Gaussian noise with
categorical corruption matrices, and its absorbing-state (masking) variant draws
an explicit line from diffusion to masked language models, the foundation later
text diffusion builds on [@austin2021d3pm]. Two flavors diverge from there.
Continuous diffusion runs in embedding space: Diffusion-LM denoises sequences of
Gaussian vectors into word vectors, and the continuous latents make gradient-based
controllable generation easy, though raw perplexity trails autoregression
[@li2022diffusionlm]. The discrete line proved more competitive. SEDD introduces
a score-entropy loss that extends score matching to discrete spaces, cutting
perplexity 25 to 75 percent over prior diffusion language models, matching or
beating GPT-2 at that scale, and trading quality for as much as 32 times fewer
network evaluations [@lou2023sedd]. All these numbers are at small scale and
author-reported.

## Scaling up, and meeting autoregression halfway

LLaDA, the masked-diffusion model @sec-diffusion introduced, is the scale data
point: an 8B diffusion language model competitive with LLaMA3-8B at in-context
learning, and ahead of GPT-4o on a narrow reversal-completion task where
bidirectional context helps [@nie2025llada]. Rather than replace autoregression,
the most practical line meets it halfway. Block diffusion is autoregressive
across blocks of tokens, which restores arbitrary-length generation and the
KV-caching of @sec-memory-scheduling, while denoising in parallel within each
block [@arriola2025blockdiffusion]. The commercial edge is already shipping:
Inception Labs' Mercury, a diffusion language model, reports throughputs above a
thousand tokens per second on an H100 and up to ten times the speed of
speed-optimized autoregressive models at comparable quality, though as an
unaudited vendor report those numbers should be read with care [@khanna2025mercury].

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether diffusion and non-autoregressive models will overtake autoregression for
text is unsettled. The case for them is parallel decoding for latency,
bidirectional context for infilling and reversal, and a quality gap that keeps
shrinking. The case against is that every frontier model is still
autoregressive, that autoregression has mature KV-caching, serving, and scaling
laws behind it, and that the parallel speedup partly erodes once you add the
refinement rounds quality needs. Most 2025 evidence is at small-to-mid scale or
self-reported vendor throughput, so treat diffusion text as a fast-moving
challenger, not a settled successor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The serving substrate reaches back into the generation paradigm. Part of
autoregression's dominance is that the KV cache of @sec-memory-scheduling makes
each next token cheap, an efficiency a naive non-autoregressive decoder forfeits
by recomputing the sequence each round. Block diffusion exists precisely to win
KV-caching back. Which generative paradigm is viable is shaped by what the
serving layer can cache, the same constraint that runs through the rest of the
book.
:::
